Featuring a book, music and lyrics by Cinco Paul, who adapted the first season of the Apple TV series he co-created , this loving send-up (and gentle skewering) of Golden Age musicals keeps the belly laughs and earworms rolling.

The effervescent stage show, from creator Cinco Paul and director-choreographer Christoper Gattelli, is all but irresistible — a giddy love letter to the form that’s enough to turn even the most skeptical curmudgeon into a walking heart-eye emoji.

Schmigadoon! delivers exactly what it promises: good old-fashioned musical fun.

Broadway performances, despite their sensational acting and writing, often follow a certain set of conventions. However, “Every Brilliant Thing” shatters the format, making it a true breath of fresh air. The difficult topics of depression and suicide are referenced throughout the show’s script.

But what about your marriage?! I hear you holler. Well, we met in the college library. He lent me Twilight and I lent him Percy Jackson and the Olympians. (We were into YA, I guess.) He took me to meet his parents, who seemed great — they played and sang jazz around the piano.
“Schmigadoon!” has scaled the pinnacle of pastiche!
The evening’s spirit is exuberantly affectionate.
Schmigadoon!, based on the first season of the Apple Original series, is a bright, pleasant diversion from whatever real world villainy is bedeviling you at the moment.

Those who haven't seen the TV show will receive Schmigadoon! as an uncomplicated good time, both an affectionate send-up of shows still performed at American high schools everywhere and a tribute to why they endure.
Yet launching a conversation around mental health with an audience magnet as powerful as Radcliffe is on balance an excellent thing.
It's exuberant, clever, eager to please, dexterously devised, and yet, with all that technique behind it, it lands in a place that's awfully unambitious.
But the musical with a book, music and lyrics by Cinco Paul is confused as to what it’s supposed to be.
It certainly adds to the enjoyment if you know the plots of the great musicals from the Golden Age and can hum “Climb Ev’ry Mountain” and “I Cain’t Say No.”
After 150 minutes of near-constant smiles, you may find yourself wishing — unlike Josh — that the bridge out of Schmigadoon stayed closed just a little longer.

Paul, the stage show’s sole author and composer, has maintained every one of the original property’s hilarious and charming treasures while making the work of condensing six television episodes into a well-paced stage musical look effortless.

A loving, winking, unabashedly cheesy valentine to Golden Age musicals, Schmigadoon! cherry-picks plotlines, melodies, and archetypes from Broadway classics like Oklahoma!, Carousel, The Music Man, and Brigadoon, creating a playful and affectionate homage to the genre.
It belongs on the stage, free from the confines and two-dimensionality of the small screen.
Schmigadoon! is a pure delight for any fan of musical theatre, both beautiful to behold and guaranteed to make you smile and laugh.
It’s hard to imagine any musical theater lover not having a good time at this candy-coated confection.

Granted, I was very close to the stage, but it still felt like Herrin, Macmillan, and Radcliffe were able to envelop all 970 of us in this small, personal story. I can’t begin to imagine the logistics required to get each performance going, let alone the infinite hours of pre-production planning.
We need it, and Schmigadoon! supplies it.

By the end of the funny and moving evening, you’ll probably be thinking of your own ideas to add to the list of things for which life is worth living. And right near the top should be Every Brilliant Thing.

Radcliffe, who has demonstrated increasing power as an actor since his inescapable cinema origins, is so perfect in the role—and so suited to the play—that a spectator might think Every Brilliant Thing built for and molded upon him. Not so.
This is a show made by people who clearly love musicals, for audiences who do too.

The actor is a revelation, though I guess it shouldn’t come as a surprise that someone who could have retired a multimillionaire at 22 but keeps pushing himself into new challenges really does love what he gets to do for a living. Beside Radcliffe’s magnetic charisma, it’s his palpable joy in the project that shines brightest.
“Schmigadoon” is sort of like “The Book of Mormon” and more like “Forbidden Broadway,” and, like both, it made me laugh.
For all its genuine affection and giddy humor, this staging only left me wistful that they don’t make them like that anymore—at least, not at the rate they used to.
At nearly two-and-a-half hours, the endless quoting from other sources becomes self-defeating; this is an evening of footnotes in search of a primary source.
The reliance on parody is both the show’s strength and its limitation.

“Schmigadoon!” on stage is no “Death Becomes Her.” It is a photo-copy replica of the TV show’s first season, in which two doctors from New York go on a camping trip in the Catskills, only to end up in a musical comprised of songs and plot points from famous shows of the 1940s and ’50s, most specific...
From the irreverent, irresistible songs to the epiphanic dream ballet, Schmigadoon! understands the brief and executes it to perfection.
A joyous musical escape that earns its happy ending.
It arrives with a superb confidence, fully aware of the traditions it is drawing from, and just as eager to run wild and free with them.
It is simply an innocent, twisted, delightful and fun-filled musical, with an incredible cast gathered to deliver the goods.
It’s goofy, big-hearted, and exactly as clever as it needs to be.
Schmigadoon! is a delightful musical romp into a fantasy land where people really do burst into song spontaneously.
Schmigadoon! is a show by and for musical mavens — and they should climb any mountain, never walk alone, and rock the boat to get themselves a seat.
Both musicals are incredibly entertaining and have a mad fab talented ensemble working their respective Broadway butts off singing and dancing and sillying at the speed of sound.
Schmigadoon! is a charming love letter, even if it packs less punch than its foreparents.
Radcliffe and the audience mesmerized by him remain buoyant, thanks to improvisation woven throughout.
Schmigadoon! is a breath of sunshine, a feel-good musical-comedy that left us smiling.
From top to bottom, Schmigadoon! is a magical delight, parodying the best in golden era musical theatre while painting its own raunchy, distinct identity.
It’s consistently funny, and it ranks among the season’s best new musicals.
This production is made with real craft and care.
Bottom line: see it, even if you missed the TV show.
Without a doubt, Schmigadoon was one of the most delightful musicals I've seen.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this affectionate Golden Age musical parody, praising its infectious charm, sharp wit, and energetic performances. While some find the meta-humor wears thin or feels derivative, most agree it's irresistibly fun for theater lovers.

sg.ra: The Nederlander is a relatively compact 1,232-seat 1921 Walter C. Jordan house (architect William Neil Smith) with a shallow orchestra rake, so you want to sit forward of where the problems begin; center rows B-E sit forward of the mezz overhang (which becomes notable at row M) and forward of where the shallow rake starts costing shorter patrons their sightlines, giving a direct center look at the 86-ft-wide stage.

sg.vl: Smart value under the overhang line
sg.ra: The Nederlander mezz overhang is 'notable by row M and cuts into the stage at row Q,' so center rows L-O sit just on the safe side of that line - you get a sub-premium price in a 1921 house known historically for being overlooked on its lone 41st Street block (the southernmost Broadway theater), without the shallow-rake head-blocking that plagues the back half.

sg.vl: Where the overhang eats the stage
sg.ra: This is the Nederlander-specific trap: the mezz overhang 'cuts into the stage at row Q,' and the 1921 orchestra's shallow rake means a tall patron in front of you is a real problem - one Redwood patron reported the overhang 'cuts off about the top 20% of the stage,' which mattered because that show featured climbing a redwood; skip for anything with vertical staging or flying effects.

The Nederlander's mezz is raked steeply enough that sightlines stay clean even though you're in a 1921 house without an elevator - rows BB and CC beat row AA because AA has a safety bar across the front that 'may be too high for shorter theatergoers' and 'can cut into the stage'; the center front mezz here looks down into the 40-ft proscenium cleanly.

Multiple guides single out the last two front-mezz rows (DD, EE) as the best 'value for money' at the Nederlander - you're still in the front mezz bloc with the steep mezz rake that keeps the 1921 house's sightlines clean, but priced below rows AA-CC; the tradeoff is legroom which is tight across the mezz here.

The Nederlander has no balcony - the rear mezz is the top tier - and the house is a compact 1,232 seats, so even the 'farthest' seat isn't far; the mezz rake stays steep enough that middle seats FF-JJ hold up, and this is the southernmost Broadway theater (208 W 41st, unusually isolated from the 44th-45th Street cluster), which typically keeps these prices lower than comparable rear-mezz at flagship houses.

sg.vl: Last rows of a no-elevator house
sg.ra: The Nederlander has 'no elevators or escalators' - a 1921 house quirk that matters when you're climbing to rows KK-PP - and a Tripadvisor thread flagged that row JJ sits above a stairwell entryway with a railing bar that can intrude; beyond JJ you're in the last stretch of a 10-row rear mezz (FF-PP) with tight legroom and the most angled sightlines in the house, and this is the top tier since there's no balcony.
